claims.text: The investigated alloy is equimolar WTaTiVZr.
WTaTiVZr has a disordered, single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain relative to commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
WTaTiVZr has enhanced toughness relative to commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
The plastic strain and toughness advantage of WTaTiVZr is governed by increased edge-dislocation mobility.
Chemical disorder and inherent lattice distortion enable increased edge-dislocation mobility in WTaTiVZr.
Atomic-size differences among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr create localized lattice distortions.
Localized lattice distortions in WTaTiVZr reduce the Peierls barrier for dislocation glide.
Increased dislocation mobility produces more homogeneous and distributed plastic deformation.
Distributed plasticity delays crack initiation and thereby increases toughness.
Plastic deformation or creep in TaTiVWZr is dislocation dominated.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a lower high-temperature creep rate than pure tungsten under identical loading.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit more uniform dislocation activity and delayed failure relative to pure tungsten.
Commercially pure tungsten at high temperature exhibits limited plastic deformation.
Commercially pure tungsten at high temperature exhibits localized dislocation activity and earlier crack initiation, leading to lower toughness.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate above approximately 800 °C when grain sizes and defect densities are comparable.
Differences in processing or testing conditions may change the balance of deformation mechanisms.
Matching temperature, strain rate, grain size, and defect condition between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten will isolate chemical complexity and lattice distortion as the cause of any observed difference.
The relative contributions of edge and other dislocation types may depend on processing and microstructural heterogeneity.
